title: What is bucketing (`df.write.bucketBy(n, "col").sortBy("col2").saveAsTable(...)`) — dividing data into a fixed number of files using hash-modulo on the bucketing column — and how does it differ from partitioning (fixed number of files vs variable directories)?
shortTitle: Bucketing (`bucketBy`) and how it differs from partitioning

s1_definition.profdef: Bucketing divides a dataset into a fixed number of files, called buckets, by applying a hash-modulo on the bucketing column so that all rows with the same key value always land in the same bucket, and it is declared with `df.write.bucketBy(n, "col").sortBy("col2").saveAsTable(name)`. Unlike partitioning, which creates a variable number of directories named by column value, bucketing always produces exactly the number of files you specify regardless of the column's cardinality. This makes bucketing suitable for high-cardinality join and aggregation keys where partitioning would explode into millions of directories.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, partitioning is like labelling drawers by branch — the number of drawers grows with the number of branches. Bucketing is like deciding up front to use exactly thirty-two drawers and dropping each account's records into a drawer chosen by a fixed rule — the last few digits of the account number, say. No matter how many accounts exist, there are always exactly thirty-two drawers, and the same account always goes to the same drawer, so when you later need to match two sets of records by account, you only compare drawer one with drawer one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Bucketing hashes a column into a fixed number of files so the same key always lands in the same bucket, giving join and aggregation benefits without the directory explosion of partitioning.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Bucketing divides a dataset into a fixed number of files, called buckets, by applying a hash-modulo on the bucketing column so that all rows with the same key value always land in the same bucket, and it is declared with `df.write.bucketBy(n, "col").sortBy("col2").saveAsTable(name)`. Unlike partitioning, which creates a variable number of directories named by column value, bucketing always produces exactly the number of files you specify regardless of the column's cardinality. This makes bucketing suitable for high-cardinality join and aggregation keys where partitioning would explode into millions of directories.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, partitioning is like labelling drawers by branch — the number of drawers grows with the number of branches. Bucketing is like deciding up front to use exactly thirty-two drawers and dropping each account's records into a drawer chosen by a fixed rule — the last few digits of the account number, say. No matter how many accounts exist, there are always exactly thirty-two drawers, and the same account always goes to the same drawer, so when you later need to match two sets of records by account, you only compare drawer one with drawer one.

**One line to remember:** Bucketing hashes a column into a fixed number of files so the same key always lands in the same bucket, giving join and aggregation benefits without the directory explosion of partitioning.

sections.s2_technical:
Bucketing assigns each row to a bucket using `hash(bucketColumn) % numBuckets`. Because the hash is deterministic, every row with the same key value lands in the same bucket number, and the number of buckets is fixed by you, not by the data. You declare it at write time with `bucketBy(numBuckets, column)` and you must use `saveAsTable`, because bucketing metadata — the bucket column, the bucket count, and the sort column — has to be registered in the catalog so later queries know the layout. You can also add `sortBy` to keep each bucket sorted by another column, which speeds up merge-based operations.

The key difference from partitioning is the output shape. Partitioning creates a directory per distinct value, so the directory count equals the cardinality and is variable. Bucketing creates a fixed number of files set by you, independent of cardinality. That is precisely why bucketing is safe for high-cardinality keys like account id: thirty-two or two hundred fifty-six buckets stay thirty-two or two hundred fifty-six files no matter how many accounts exist, avoiding directory explosion and the small-file problem.

The benefits appear at read time for operations on the bucketing column. If two tables are bucketed on the same column with the same bucket count, a join on that column needs no shuffle: Spark knows matching keys are co-located in the same bucket number on both sides, so it joins bucket to bucket directly. Similarly, a groupBy on the bucketing column avoids a shuffle because each bucket already contains all rows for its keys. And because the layout is hash-based, Spark can do bucket pruning for equality filters on the bucketing column, reading only the bucket a value hashes to.

A senior-level nuance is the requirements and caveats. Bucketing works best on high-cardinality columns that are your join or group keys, which is the opposite of partitioning's low-cardinality rule. Both tables in a bucket-aware join must share the same bucket count and column. The metadata only lives in the catalog, so you must use saveAsTable and read through the catalog table, not a raw path. And classic Hive-style bucketing is not supported for Delta tables, which use their own clustering mechanisms instead. You can also combine bucketing with partitioning — partition by a low-cardinality column and bucket by a high-cardinality key within each partition.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India frequently joins the large transactions table to the large accounts table on account id. Both are huge, so every join shuffles both tables across the network, which is slow and expensive. Partitioning by account id is impossible because there are millions of accounts. This is exactly what bucketing solves — bucketing both tables by account id into the same number of buckets means the join can match bucket to bucket with no shuffle.

Problem 2 — Reports also group transactions by account id to compute per-account totals. A groupBy on account id normally shuffles. This is exactly what bucketing solves — because each bucket holds all rows for its account ids, the aggregation runs per bucket with no shuffle.

The demo models how rows map to a fixed number of buckets via hash-modulo, shows that both tables place the same account in the same bucket, and proves that a bucket-to-bucket join needs no cross-bucket comparison, logging the bucket assignments and the shuffle-free join plan.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four account ids, with both the transactions table and the accounts table bucketed by account id into eight buckets.

Step 1: For each account, the bucket assigner computes `floorMod(hash(accountId), 8)`. Because the hash is deterministic, SAV2001 produces the same bucket number every time.

Step 2: The same computation runs for the accounts table. Since the formula and bucket count are identical, SAV2001 lands in the same bucket number on both tables.

Step 3: The demo logs each account's bucket on both tables side by side and confirms they match, which is the condition for a shuffle-free bucket-to-bucket join.

Step 4: The demo verifies all four accounts matched and logs that the join can proceed bucket to bucket without any network shuffle, and that the layout stays at eight fixed buckets regardless of how many accounts exist, so there is no directory explosion.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:29:30 [INFO] bucketBy(8, "accountId") on BOTH tables:
2026-10-30 04:29:30 [INFO] SAV2001 -> transactions bucket 3, accounts bucket 3  (SAME → shuffle-free join)
2026-10-30 04:29:30 [INFO] CUR3001 -> transactions bucket 6, accounts bucket 6  (SAME → shuffle-free join)
2026-10-30 04:29:30 [INFO] SAV2002 -> transactions bucket 1, accounts bucket 1  (SAME → shuffle-free join)
2026-10-30 04:29:30 [INFO] CUR3002 -> transactions bucket 4, accounts bucket 4  (SAME → shuffle-free join)
2026-10-30 04:29:30 [INFO] Every account lands in the same bucket on both tables — join bucket-to-bucket, NO shuffle.
2026-10-30 04:29:30 [INFO] Fixed 8 buckets regardless of millions of accounts — no directory explosion.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Bucketing divides a dataset into a fixed number of files by hashing a column and taking the modulo of the bucket count, so every row with the same key value always lands in the same bucket number. I declare it at write time with bucketBy, giving the number of buckets and the column, optionally adding sortBy to keep each bucket sorted, and I must use saveAsTable because the bucketing metadata — the column, the count, and the sort order — has to be registered in the catalog for later queries to exploit it.

The fundamental difference from partitioning is the output shape. Partitioning creates one directory per distinct value, so the number of directories grows with the column's cardinality and is variable. Bucketing creates exactly the number of files I choose, independent of cardinality. That is why bucketing is the right tool for high-cardinality keys like account id, where partitioning would explode into millions of directories, bloat metadata, and crash the driver. Two hundred fifty-six buckets stay two hundred fifty-six files whether there are a thousand accounts or ten million.

The payoff is at read time for operations on the bucketing column. When two tables are bucketed on the same column with the same bucket count, a join on that column needs no shuffle, because Spark knows matching keys sit in the same bucket number on both sides and can join bucket to bucket directly. A groupBy on the bucketing column likewise avoids a shuffle. At the National Bank of India we bucketed the transactions and accounts tables by account id into the same number of buckets, and the daily join that used to shuffle two huge tables became shuffle-free, cutting the runtime sharply. The way I summarize it in interviews is that partitioning is for low-cardinality columns you filter on and gives pruning through directories, while bucketing is for high-cardinality columns you join or group on and gives shuffle-free joins through a fixed number of hash files — and the caveats are that both sides must share the bucket count and column, you must use saveAsTable, and classic bucketing is not supported on Delta tables.
